paras: The exclusion of William Floyd from his Oklahoma City home was a 1919 episode in which police, enforcing a segregation ordinance, arrested a Black man for moving into a house he had bought on a white-majority block and kept him out of it under armed guard. After a month of court hearings, the charge was dismissed in mid-June and Floyd moved in despite a published statement that the house would be dynamited. The Black Dispatch followed the case weekly, publicizing a city attorney's courtroom remark about "DEAD NIGGERS" and hailing the dismissal as "a decisive victory for Black Manhood."

According to the petition Floyd later filed in federal court, he bought two lots in the military addition to Oklahoma City in early January 1919 and took possession of them as his family residence on May 12. The Black Dispatch placed the house in the 200 block of East Second Street and reported that Floyd, who ran a shoe repair shop with his wife, had worked two years to pay for it. A. Baxter Whitby, president of the local NAACP branch, later wrote that Floyd bought it from a white owner, near the Breaux Theatre in the heart of the Black community.

Police arrested Floyd the day after he moved in and jailed him until the Black Dispatch editor Dunjee and Dr. A. P. Bethel secured his bond. His petition stated that he was then arrested again, warned by police not to occupy the house, and that armed guards were placed around it. On May 19 almost 400 Black residents met at Tabernacle Baptist Church, heard Floyd describe his arrest, placed the case with the NAACP branch, and collected $168.

At a hearing in the federal court at Guthrie on May 27, Floyd's counsel E. T. Barbour argued that an agreement made in the city court removed the police only on condition that Floyd stay out, so that "THE AGREEMENT ITSELF BARS MR. FLOYD FROM HIS OWN HOME." On June 3, the Black Dispatch reported, Judge John H. Cottrell called the ordinance "in plain violation of the constitution of the United States" but denied a temporary injunction without prejudice for want of a showing of irreparable damage.

At Floyd's police-court trial before Judge Munden on June 7, city counsel E. J. Giddings warned that "if these people don't stop meddling with our ordinances there is going to be a lot of DEAD NIGGERS around you." On Tuesday, June 17, Munden dismissed the case, ruling that Floyd "has not violated any of the city's ordinances." Floyd moved into the house the next day, "despite the published statements in a local sheet to the effect that the house would be dynamited."

The Black Dispatch argued that the city had, by its own acknowledgment, wrongfully and forcibly ejected Floyd from his home and was liable for heavy damages. By late June Whitby reported that more than $300 had been raised and that officials had drawn up a "more stringent Segregation Ordinance," while the Black Dispatch mocked city attorney Ross Lillard's proposed health ordinance to replace "the repudiated segregation farce."

The Black Dispatch of Oklahoma City, whose editor had helped secure Floyd's bond, reported each stage on its front page. Its headlines included "Negroes Fight Unfair Ordinance," "Federal Court Smites City," and "White Attorney Says Favorable Decision For Blacks Will Mean A Lot Of Dead Niggers." Its June 20 editorial paired the dynamite statement with the attorney's remark as signs of "the spirit of mob violence." The same editorial called the dismissal "a decisive victory for Black Manhood" and advised Black residents to "suffer no intimidation."

The Tulsa Star reported the mass meeting under the headline "BIG FIGHT STARTS IN CAPITAY CITY." A Guthrie dispatch summarizing Floyd's petition ran in the Cleveland Advocate on June 14 and the Plaindealer on July 4, calling him only "a race man" and omitting the threats.

Munden reportedly said out of court that he considered the ordinance valid but found the block was not 75 percent white-owned, a count the Black Dispatch disputed. The Guthrie dispatch dated the federal ruling to a Thursday, while the Black Dispatch placed it on Tuesday, June 3.

reader.title: Exclusion of William Floyd from his Oklahoma City home
bases: Police enforcing a segregation ordinance arrested Floyd, put armed guards on his house and kept him out of it, a white paper published that the house would be dynamited, and a city attorney spoke in court of 'dead' Negroes; no one was reported hurt and no attack on the house was reported (A6, A7, A8, A9).

The arrest and exclusion are reported independently by the Black Dispatch, the Tulsa Star and a Guthrie wire dispatch (A2, A7, A8, A13); the dynamite threat itself is reported only by the Black Dispatch (A8, A9).

accounts.label: Black Dispatch reports
accounts.gist: Floyd was arrested and kept from his home for over a month by the city; the city court dismissed the case and he moved in despite a white paper's statement that the house would be dynamited.

accounts.label: Floyd's petition (Guthrie wire dispatch)
accounts.gist: Floyd bought two lots in January, took possession May 12, was arrested, rearrested after bail, ordered not to occupy the house, and armed guards were placed around it.

accounts.label: City's claim
accounts.gist: City counsel said Floyd bought the property to force the other owners to sell at a loss; Judge Munden reportedly said the ordinance was valid but the block was not 75 percent white-owned.

framing.detail: The Black Dispatch headlined 'Negroes Fight Unfair Ordinance' and 'White Attorney Says Favorable Decision For Blacks Will Mean A Lot Of Dead Niggers', and its editorials linked the threats to 'the spirit of mob violence'.
The Tulsa Star called Floyd 'the late victim of the Oklahoma City segregation ordinance' and reported the meeting's 'indignation'.
The Guthrie dispatch in the Cleveland Advocate and Plaindealer summarized Floyd's petition neutrally and did not mention the threats.

conflicts.note: Two printings of the same Guthrie dispatch; likely a typesetting or OCR difference. The Tulsa Star's 'last week' (from May 22) fits either.
The Black Dispatch, which reported from the Guthrie hearings, is the more detailed source.

versions.value: Judge Munden: the block was not 75 percent white-owned, so Floyd did not violate the ordinance
Black Dispatch: only two other Black owners in the block besides Floyd
Whitby: the house was in the heart of the Black community and many houses on the block were rentals

conflicts.note: Accounts of the block's racial make-up differ.

record_check.dossier: Arrest May 13 (or 15), 1919; exclusion until the case was dismissed June 17; dynamite statement published before Floyd moved in on June 18.
Arrest, jailing and rearrest; armed police guard keeping him out of his house; a published dynamite threat; a courtroom threat of killings by city counsel.
Oklahoma City police and officials enforced the exclusion; the dynamite statement came from an unnamed white local paper, attributed to unnamed whites.
Officers (police, city officials) for the exclusion; unknown for the dynamite threat.
Floyd was arrested and jailed briefly, then out on bond; not in custody when the dynamite statement appeared.

record_check.record: A local newspaper published statements that William Floyd's house ... would be dynamited. Floyd moved in anyway.
record_check.dossier: Correct as far as it goes, but the threat was the end of a month-long exclusion by police under the segregation ordinance, contested in police and federal courts.
At least 9 distinct Black-press items in 4 papers (Black Dispatch, Tulsa Star, Cleveland Advocate, Plaindealer), May 23-July 4.

info: Floyd took possession May 12, 1919, and was arrested the next day (May 13 in one printing, May 15 in another); the city court dismissed the case Tuesday, June 17, and Floyd moved in Wednesday, June 18, despite the published dynamite threat.
Floyd's house in the 'military addition' to Oklahoma City, in the 200 block of East Second Street, near the Breaux Theatre.
William Floyd, a Black ('colored', 'Negro') property owner, and his wife.
Charged with violating Oklahoma City's segregation ordinance by moving into a house he bought in a block with a white majority.
Oklahoma City police and city officials enforcing the segregation ordinance; the dynamite statement appeared in an unnamed white local paper, attributed to unnamed whites.

Judge Munden dismissed the case, ruling Floyd 'has not violated any of the city's ordinances'; Floyd moved in. Federal judge Cottrell denied a temporary injunction without prejudice but said the ordinance violated the Constitution.
